name: Ancient Egypt
summary: Civilisation along the lower Nile ruled by pharaohs for about three thousand years, from the unification of the Two Lands to the Roman annexation after Cleopatra.

name: Assyria
summary: Mesopotamian kingdom on the upper Tigris that became the largest empire of its time in the 9th–7th centuries BCE, known for its army and for deporting conquered peoples.

name: Babylonia
summary: Akkadian-speaking state of southern Mesopotamia, famous for the law code of Hammurabi and for the later Neo-Babylonian empire of Nebuchadnezzar II.

name: Kingdom of Kush
summary: Nubian kingdom south of Egypt, centred first at Napata and later Meroë. Its kings ruled Egypt as the 25th dynasty in the 8th century BCE.

name: Meroë
summary: Later capital of the Kushite kingdom on the middle Nile, a centre of iron working and of Nubian pyramids, which declined in the 4th century CE.

name: Elam
summary: Civilisation in south-western Iran with its own language and script, a long-time rival of Mesopotamian states until it was absorbed by the Persians.

name: Urartu
summary: Iron Age kingdom around Lake Van in the Armenian highlands, known for fortresses and irrigation works and for its wars with Assyria.

name: Hittite Empire
summary: Anatolian power that rivalled Egypt in the Late Bronze Age. It collapsed around 1180 BCE during the wider upheavals of the eastern Mediterranean.

name: Kingdom of David and Solomon
summary: Biblical kingdom of Israel under Saul, David and Solomon. Historians disagree on how large and how unified it really was.

name: Kingdom of Saba
summary: South Arabian kingdom that grew rich on the incense trade and on the Marib dam, remembered in tradition through the queen of Sheba.

name: Zhou dynasty
summary: Chinese dynasty whose kings gradually lost real power to the regional states of the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods, when Confucius and other thinkers lived.

name: State of Qin
summary: Western state of the Zhou world that conquered its rivals in the 3rd century BCE and became the base of the first unified Chinese empire.

name: Han dynasty
summary: Chinese empire that followed Qin, which shaped Chinese administration and identity and opened the Silk Road trade to Central Asia.

name: Tang dynasty
summary: Chinese empire often seen as a golden age of poetry, trade and cosmopolitan city life, with a capital that was among the largest cities in the world.

name: Song dynasty
summary: Chinese empire of great commercial and technical growth, with printing, gunpowder weapons and paper money, but under constant military pressure from northern neighbours.

name: Liao dynasty
summary: Khitan-led empire of Manchuria, Mongolia and northern China that ruled both nomads and farmers through two separate systems of government.

name: Ming dynasty
summary: Chinese dynasty that expelled the Mongols, rebuilt the Great Wall and the Forbidden City, and sent the treasure fleets of Zheng He across the Indian Ocean.

name: Qing dynasty
summary: Last imperial dynasty of China, founded by the Manchus. It roughly doubled China's territory and fell in 1912 after the 1911 revolution.

name: Mongol Empire
summary: Largest contiguous land empire in history, founded by Genghis Khan, which split into four khanates within a few decades of his grandsons' reigns.

name: Golden Horde
summary: Western khanate of the Mongol Empire that ruled the steppe north of the Black and Caspian Seas and collected tribute from the Russian principalities.

name: Chagatai Khanate
summary: Central Asian khanate inherited by Genghis Khan's second son, which split into western and eastern halves and gradually adopted Turkic and Islamic ways.

name: Xiongnu
summary: Powerful confederation of steppe nomads north of China, whose rivalry with the Han dynasty helped shape the early Silk Road.

name: Hunnic Empire
summary: Steppe empire that reached Europe in the 4th century and under Attila raided both halves of the Roman Empire before breaking up soon after his death.

name: Achaemenid Empire
summary: First Persian empire, founded by Cyrus the Great, which stretched from Egypt and Anatolia to the Indus and fell to Alexander the Great.

name: Parthian Empire
summary: Iranian empire that controlled the land between Rome and China for almost five centuries and held back Roman armies on the eastern frontier.

name: Sasanian Empire
summary: Last pre-Islamic Persian empire, a state-backed Zoroastrian rival of Rome and Byzantium until the Arab conquests.

name: Qajar Iran
summary: Turkic-origin dynasty that ruled Persia through the 19th century, losing land to Russia and Britain and facing the 1906 constitutional revolution.

name: Empire of Alexander the Great
summary: Short-lived empire from Greece to the Indus built by Alexander III of Macedon in about thirteen years and divided among his generals after his death.

name: Carthaginian Empire
summary: Phoenician-founded maritime power in North Africa that dominated the western Mediterranean until Rome destroyed the city in 146 BCE.

name: Roman Republic
summary: Rome as a state governed by elected magistrates and a senate, which conquered Italy and then the Mediterranean before civil wars ended it.

name: Roman Empire
summary: Mediterranean empire ruled by emperors from Augustus onward. Its western half ended in 476 CE; the eastern half lasted as the Byzantine Empire.

name: Western Roman Empire
summary: The western half of the Roman Empire after the division of 395, which lost most of its provinces to Germanic kingdoms before its last emperor was deposed.

name: Byzantine Empire
summary: The continuing eastern Roman Empire, Greek-speaking and Orthodox Christian, ruled from Constantinople until the Ottoman conquest in 1453.

name: Franks
summary: Germanic people who settled in northern Gaul and under the Merovingians and Carolingians created the most lasting successor state of Rome in the west.

name: Visigoths
summary: Gothic people who sacked Rome in 410 and then ruled Gaul and Hispania until the Muslim conquest of Spain.

name: Ostrogoths
summary: Gothic people who formed a kingdom in Italy under Theoderic the Great before Byzantine armies reconquered it.

name: Carolingian Empire
summary: Frankish empire revived under Charlemagne, crowned emperor in 800, which covered much of western and central Europe and split by the Treaty of Verdun in 843.

name: Holy Roman Empire
summary: Loose union of German and neighbouring lands under an elected emperor, lasting from Otto I's coronation until Napoleon's wars.

name: Papal States
summary: Territories in central Italy ruled directly by the popes until they were absorbed into the Kingdom of Italy.

name: Republic of Venice
summary: Maritime republic in a lagoon at the head of the Adriatic, run by an elected doge and merchant families, which dominated Mediterranean trade for centuries.

name: Kingdom of France
summary: Monarchy that grew from the lands around Paris into one of Europe's strongest states, ending with the French Revolution.

name: Kingdom of England
summary: Monarchy covering most of the island of Great Britain's south, which merged with Scotland in 1707 to form Great Britain.

name: Kingdom of Portugal
summary: Atlantic monarchy that led European exploration in the 15th century and built a trading empire from Brazil to Asia.

name: Denmark–Norway
summary: Union of the Danish and Norwegian crowns under one king, which also held Iceland, Greenland and colonies overseas.

name: Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth
summary: Large union of Poland and Lithuania with an elected king and a powerful noble parliament, partitioned out of existence by its neighbours.

name: Grand Duchy of Moscow
summary: Russian principality that gathered the surrounding lands, threw off Mongol overlordship and became the core of the Russian state.

name: Russian Empire
summary: Empire spanning Eastern Europe, Siberia and parts of Central Asia, ruled by tsars until the revolutions of 1917.

name: Soviet Union
summary: One-party federal state created after the Russian Revolution, a superpower of the Cold War that dissolved into fifteen republics in 1991.

name: Kingdom of Prussia
summary: German monarchy known for its army and administration, which led the unification of Germany in 1871.

name: Austro-Hungarian Empire
summary: Dual monarchy of Austria and Hungary under the Habsburgs, home to many nationalities, which broke up after losing the First World War.

name: Emirate of Córdoba
summary: Muslim state in Iberia founded by an Umayyad prince who escaped the Abbasid takeover, and which became a caliphate in 929.

name: Abbasid Caliphate
summary: Islamic caliphate ruled from Baghdad, a centre of learning and trade, whose real power faded long before the Mongols took Baghdad in 1258.

name: Fatimid Caliphate
summary: Ismaili Shia caliphate that conquered Egypt in 969, founded Cairo and rivalled the Abbasids for leadership of the Muslim world.

name: Almohad Caliphate
summary: Berber reform movement turned empire that ruled Morocco, the Maghreb and Muslim Spain until Christian and local rivals broke it up.

name: Ottoman Empire
summary: Turkish-led empire that took Constantinople in 1453 and ruled much of south-eastern Europe, western Asia and North Africa for six centuries.

name: Mamluk Sultanate
summary: Egyptian and Syrian state ruled by former slave soldiers, who defeated the Mongols at Ain Jalut in 1260 and lasted until the Ottoman conquest.

name: Delhi Sultanate
summary: Series of Muslim dynasties ruling much of northern India from Delhi until the Mughal conquest of 1526.

name: Vijayanagara Empire
summary: South Indian Hindu empire with a rich capital at Hampi, which stood against the northern sultanates until its defeat at Talikota in 1565.

name: Chola dynasty
summary: South Indian dynasty whose medieval emperors, notably Rajaraja I and Rajendra I, built a navy that reached Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia.

name: Gupta Empire
summary: North Indian empire of the 4th–6th centuries, remembered for achievements in mathematics, astronomy, literature and art.

name: Srivijaya
summary: Buddhist maritime empire based on Sumatra that controlled the Strait of Malacca and so the sea trade between India and China.

name: Khmer Empire
summary: Southeast Asian empire centred on Angkor, builder of Angkor Wat and a vast water-management system, which declined in the 14th–15th centuries.

name: Ayutthaya Kingdom
summary: Thai kingdom that became a major trading power of Southeast Asia until it was sacked by Burmese armies in 1767.

name: Tibetan Empire
summary: Imperial Tibet, whose armies at times reached into Central Asia and the Tang capital and which adopted Buddhism before breaking apart.

name: Silla
summary: Korean kingdom that, allied with Tang China, unified most of the peninsula in the 7th century and was a centre of Buddhist art.

name: Joseon
summary: Korean dynasty that ruled for over five hundred years under Confucian principles, and which created the Hangul alphabet in the 15th century.

name: Empire of Japan
summary: Japanese state from the Meiji Restoration to the end of the Second World War, which industrialised quickly and built an empire in Asia.

name: Ghana Empire
summary: West African empire that grew rich on the gold and salt trade across the Sahara. It is unrelated to the modern country except by name.

name: Mali Empire
summary: West African empire founded by Sundiata Keita, which under Mansa Musa became famous for its gold and for Timbuktu as a centre of learning.

name: Songhai Empire
summary: Largest West African empire of its time, controlling the Niger trade routes until a Moroccan invasion in 1591.

name: Kanem–Bornu Empire
summary: Sahelian empire around Lake Chad that moved its centre west to Bornu and lasted, in changing forms, for over a thousand years counting Kanem.

name: Oyo Empire
summary: Yoruba empire of the savanna north of the forest, which used cavalry and trade to dominate its neighbours until civil war and Fulani attacks.

name: Kingdom of Benin
summary: Edo kingdom of the Guinea forest, famous for its bronze plaques and ruled by an oba until the British expedition of 1897.

name: Kingdom of Dahomey
summary: West African kingdom with a strong standing army, which took part in the Atlantic slave trade before French conquest.

name: Zulu Kingdom
summary: Southern African kingdom built by Shaka, which fought the British in 1879 and was later absorbed into the colony of Natal.

name: Kingdom of Aksum
summary: Trading kingdom in the Ethiopian highlands that minted coins, raised great stone obelisks and adopted Christianity in the 4th century.

name: Makuria
summary: Christian Nubian kingdom on the Nile that signed a long-lasting treaty with Muslim Egypt and survived into the 14th century.

name: Ethiopian Empire
summary: Christian monarchy of the Ethiopian highlands, claiming descent from Solomon, which kept its independence through the colonial era apart from a brief Italian occupation.

name: Great Zimbabwe
summary: Shona trading state of southern Africa, known for its large dry-stone enclosures and for its gold and cattle wealth.

name: Aztec Empire
summary: Alliance led by Tenochtitlan that collected tribute from much of central Mexico until Spanish and allied forces took the capital in 1521.

name: Inca Empire
summary: Largest empire of the pre-Columbian Americas, linked by roads across the Andes, which fell to Spanish conquistadors in the 1530s.

name: Wari Empire
summary: Andean state centred on Huari in the Peruvian highlands, which built roads and administrative centres centuries before the Inca.

name: Timurid Empire
summary: Central Asian empire created by Timur, whose successors made Samarkand and Herat centres of astronomy, architecture and painting.

name: Crimean Khanate
summary: Tatar khanate and Ottoman vassal on the Black Sea steppe, whose raiders reached deep into Eastern Europe until Russia annexed it.

name: Maratha Empire
summary: Indian power founded by Shivaji that overtook much of the weakening Mughal territory before the British defeated it.

name: Sikh Empire
summary: Punjabi state built by Ranjit Singh, with a modernised army, which fell to the British after two wars.
